title: run_baseline.sh accepts any listener on localhost:<port> as the model server, so another local user can supply the programs the operator executes
description:
Lower-trust principal: a second unprivileged local user (or other workload sharing the host network namespace) on the GPU host where the operator runs baselines/run_baseline.sh. Accepted input: HTTP responses from whichever process is listening on `localhost:<port>`. Control that should stop it: the launcher should only hand the frameworks an endpoint that is provably the vLLM child it started (and the frameworks should authenticate that endpoint); the only visible checks are a `curl -s localhost:$port/v1/models` probe and a `kill -0 $server` liveness test that is evaluated after the probe has already returned success. Boundary crossed: local user A to code execution as operator B. Affected resource: the operator's account (files, environment variables including any provider keys, EVAL_LOG score integrity), because every completion returned by the endpoint is turned into a program and executed by benchmarks/evaluation.py with the operator's environment.

Source-visible mechanics: (1) free_port binds ('', 0), prints the number and releases the socket; the number is reused later for `vllm serve ... --port $port`, where it is visible in the process arguments. For shinkaevolve the main port is chosen before the embedding server is started and only used after that server is up. (2) `serve` backgrounds vLLM and loops: `curl -s localhost:$port/v1/models > /dev/null && return 0; kill -0 $server || break`. Any HTTP responder satisfies the probe (no -f, no identity check), and success is returned without consulting the child's state, so a vLLM child that failed to bind because the port was taken goes unnoticed. (3) All three drivers configure the framework with `http://localhost:<port>/v1` and the placeholder key 'EMPTY'; vLLM is started without --host and without --api-key, so neither side authenticates the other and the hostname is resolved by each client. (4) The completion text becomes child_code and is executed by the shared evaluation as a subprocess that inherits the operator environment.

Two ways a foreign listener can end up answering, both needing local validation: (a) binding 127.0.0.1:<port> between the `vllm serve` exec (port visible in process arguments) and vLLM's own listen; (b) binding [::1]:<port> at any time if vLLM's default bind covers IPv4 only, with clients that resolve `localhost` to ::1 first. This is not the documented 'generated code runs unsandboxed' trade-off: the party choosing the code is a different local principal than the operator and the operator's own model. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed free_port binds and releases a port (run_baseline.sh:29), and that serve() accepts the endpoint as soon as `curl -s localhost:$port/v1/models` succeeds, a test made before the liveness check of the vLLM child in the same loop iteration (:36); no key or identity check ties the answering process to the server the script started.
claimed_root_cause: baselines/run_baseline.sh treats 'something answers HTTP on localhost:<port>' as proof that its own vLLM child is serving: the port is picked by bind-and-release, the readiness probe is evaluated before (and independently of) the child liveness test, and the server/clients share no secret and use the ambiguous hostname `localhost`, so the identity of the endpoint whose output is executed is never established.

The same port is handed to the framework driver (`--port $port`); lines 59 and 60 do the same for shinkaevolve (plus --embed-port) and codeevolve.

title: Evaluated program receives the path of the shared score log and can write records to it directly
description: EVAL_LOG is documented as the file from which every framework's scores are read. evaluation.py starts the evaluator child with the complete parent environment, so the log path exported by run_baseline.sh reaches run_evaluator.py, and the per-case children of the scientific problems and the circle_packing_26 wrapper inherit it again because they are started without an env argument. The log is an ordinary file owned by the uid that runs the program and is opened in append mode by the parent; nothing authenticates a record or restricts who appends, truncates or rewrites it. A program in any of the 21 problems, including those whose header says the child is given only the case inputs, can therefore append records with a chosen score, time and sha, or alter earlier records and the saved sources under programs/. Run directories of the other frameworks for the same problem are siblings of the log's parent directory, so the same access reaches their logs when they are on the same host. This is independent of the marker channel: moving the program out of the evaluator process would not remove it. The lower-trust principal is the LLM output; the affected resource is the integrity of the score record that the cross-framework comparison relies on. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed the child environment is {**os.environ, **SINGLE_THREAD} (evaluation.py:46), that run_baseline.sh:55 exports EVAL_LOG, and that records are appended with no integrity field (evaluation.py:72-75). This is a separate control from the metrics marker: fixing the marker does not protect the log file.
claimed_root_cause: The score record of truth is a plain file in the trust domain of the evaluated program, and evaluation.py passes its location to that program through the inherited environment; there is no integrity control on the log.

title: Evaluated program can set its own recorded score through the in-band metrics marker
description: The shared harness reads the score from the last line of the child's combined stdout and stderr that starts with the fixed marker '@@METRICS@@'. For 15 of the 21 problems the evaluator imports the LLM-generated program into the same interpreter that later prints that marker. Program code can therefore print its own marker line and end the interpreter (os._exit, or sys.exit, which the evaluators' 'except Exception' does not catch) before the genuine line is printed, or replace the evaluator's functions in memory. evaluation.py never checks the child's exit status, uses no per-run secret, and accepts any numeric non-NaN score, including values far above what the evaluator can produce. The forged value is returned to the framework as the fitness and is appended to EVAL_LOG by the trusted parent, which the file header describes as the place all frameworks' scores are read from. The lower-trust principal is the LLM output; the affected resource is the integrity of the benchmark scores and of the selection signal inside each run. The strongest control visible in source is the child process boundary with a 60 s limit, which does not separate the program from the marker's author. For the six evaluators that run the program in a further child process, the same marker channel might be reachable by a same-uid descendant that reopens the parent's stdout pipe through /proc and then stops the parent; that variant depends on operating-system behaviour and is not established from source. Reviewer note: Parent review read benchmarks/evaluation.py and benchmarks/run_evaluator.py in full: the scorer takes found[-1] among stdout lines starting with the marker (evaluation.py:50-52) and never checks the child exit status; run_evaluator.py prints the genuine marker only after module.evaluate() returns (:12-16), and in-process evaluators such as kissing_number_11 import the program into that same interpreter (evaluator.py:65-66). A harness draft exists at security/pipeline/poc/benchmarks-evaluation_inband-metrics-marker-forgery/.
claimed_root_cause: The metrics channel is unauthenticated and shared with the untrusted program: run_evaluator.py executes the program inside the process that emits the marker, and evaluation.py trusts the last marker line without checking the exit status, a per-run secret or a plausible score range.

title: Processes started by an evaluated program outlive the evaluation and its time limit
description: evaluation.py starts the evaluator in a new session and states that this lets a timeout kill everything the child started. The group kill is sent only when communicate() times out, and only to the original process group. A descendant that the program moved to another session or group is not signalled, and when the evaluation finishes normally nothing is signalled at all, so a background process that does not hold the stdout pipe keeps running with the operator's uid and environment after the score has been recorded. The per-case runner of the scientific problems has the same structure, and the circle_packing_26 evaluator kills only its direct child. Because the evaluator child is in its own session, the group SIGTERM that run_baseline.sh relies on at the end of the budget does not reach in-flight evaluations, whose only supervisor is the adapter process being terminated. The task statements promise a hard 60 s limit on one core. A surviving process is not bound by it: it can continue computing and leave results for later programs of the same lineage, act on the score log after the parent has written the genuine record, and keep running after the framework run ends. The lower-trust principal is the LLM output; the affected resources are the compute-budget rule the comparison depends on and the operator's host after the run. A related robustness effect is that the communicate() call after the kill has no timeout, so a surviving descendant that still holds the pipe keeps evaluate() from returning. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed os.killpg is called only in the TimeoutExpired branch (evaluation.py:55-56) although the comment at :41 says the process group lets a timeout kill everything the evaluator started; a descendant that calls setsid leaves the group. The concrete cross-boundary effect to test is work that continues past the 60 s limit and is consumed by a later evaluation (the per-evaluation compute budget the benchmark states).
claimed_root_cause: Process lifetime is bound to the evaluation only through a process-group SIGKILL issued in the timeout handler; there is no kill on normal completion and no containment (subreaper, cgroup or PID namespace) for descendants that leave the group.

title: Scientific-problem programs can read the reference answers they are scored against
description: scientific_cases.py states that the program's entry function runs in a child process that receives only the case inputs and never the reference answer. That is true of the arguments, but the child runs under the same uid with no file-system restriction. For convection_diffusion_2d and helmholtz_2d the answers are stored in reference.npz beside the evaluator, world-readable and keyed by case name; for burgers_1d, nonnormal_eigenvalues and sparse_linear_systems the evaluator source regenerates the references from a fixed seed, so importing that file yields them. The absolute problem directory appears in the command line of the child's parent process, and BENCHMARK_PROBLEM is in the inherited environment. A program that returns the stored reference for the case it is given has relative error 0 and receives full marks on every case without solving the problem. The lower-trust principal is the LLM output; the affected resource is the validity of the scores of the five scientific-computing problems. The control named in source is the separate child process with input-only arguments. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed the explicit claim at benchmarks/scientific_cases.py:2-5 that the child "receives only the case's inputs (never the reference answer)"; the child (CHILD, :19-29) runs under the same uid with no file-system restriction, and the score is digits of accuracy against the reference.
claimed_root_cause: Reference answers are kept in files readable by the process that runs the untrusted program, and the isolation claimed for that process covers only its arguments, not its file access or environment.

title: circle_packing_26 evaluator unpickles a results file controlled by the evaluated program
description: The circle_packing_26 evaluator is the one evaluator that runs the program in a child process of its own. The child returns its result by pickling the objects that run_packing() returned into a file next to the wrapper script, and the evaluator loads that file with pickle.load after checking only that the child exited with code 0. The objects are chosen by the program, and the program can also write the file itself because its path is the wrapper script path plus '.results'. Unpickling therefore executes program-chosen callables inside the run_evaluator.py process, which is the process that prints the metrics marker. That removes the only separation this evaluator has between the program and the scorer: code running there can emit its own metrics and end the process, and a SystemExit raised during the load is not caught by the evaluator's 'except Exception', while the child's stdout, whose lines after the first are reprinted without a prefix, has already been written. The lower-trust principal is the LLM output; the crossed boundary is child process to evaluator process; the affected resource is the integrity of this problem's scores. Both processes run under the same uid, so no additional operating-system privilege is claimed. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed run_with_timeout loads <wrapper>.results with pickle.load (circle_packing_26/evaluator.py:166-168) after checking only the child exit code. Scope of the gain: the loading process is the run_evaluator.py child that prints the metrics marker, so this is a second route to score forgery for the one evaluator that separates the program from the scorer by a process; it does not reach the framework process.
claimed_root_cause: run_with_timeout uses pickle as the result format for data produced by the untrusted child and loads it in the evaluator process with no restriction on the types that may be constructed.

title: Evaluation runs Python with the shared temp directory first on the module search path
description: The circle_packing_26 evaluator writes its wrapper script directly into the system temp directory and runs it as a script. Python then puts the script's directory, normally the world-writable /tmp, at the front of the module search path, ahead of the standard library and site-packages, and the wrapper imports numpy, pickle and traceback. A file such as numpy.py or pickle.py present in that directory is imported and executed with the operator's uid on every circle_packing_26 evaluation, under any framework. The harness sets PYTHONNOUSERSITE but not safe-path mode. The results file is a predictable sibling name in the same directory, is opened by the child without exclusive creation, and is unpickled by the evaluator whenever it exists and the child exited with 0, so on hosts without the protected-file sysctls a file placed there by another account can be loaded. The same pattern reaches the 15 in-process evaluators when OpenEvolve is the framework: OpenEvolve writes each program directly into the temp directory and the evaluators insert the program's directory at sys.path[0] before importing it, so the program's own imports of modules not yet loaded, for example jax in the shipped initial programs, resolve from the shared directory first. Two lower-trust principals are affected differently. Another local account on a shared host could plant such a file and gain code execution as the operator; whether such accounts and a shared /tmp exist is a deployment fact. An evaluated program can plant one and thereby persist into every later evaluation and run on the host. The affected resources are the operator's account and the integrity of later evaluations. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".py", delete=False) with no dir (evaluator.py:95) and that the file is run as [sys.executable, temp_file_path] (:148), which puts the temp directory first on sys.path before the wrapper's `import numpy`. evaluation.py changes the child's cwd, not TMPDIR.
claimed_root_cause: Scripts and result files are created directly in the shared temp directory instead of a private directory, and the interpreters are started without isolated or safe-path mode, so the shared directory becomes an import location.

title: CodeEvolve's shipped model templates disable TLS certificate verification for the client that carries the API key and returns code to execute
description: Both real-model configuration templates vendored under baselines/CodeEvolve/configs/templates/ set verify_ssl: False on every language-model role (exploration ensemble, exploitation ensemble, sampler auxiliary model). CodeEvolve passes each entry straight into OpenAILM, which builds httpx.AsyncClient(verify=self.verify_ssl) and gives it to AsyncOpenAI together with the operator's API_KEY and API_BASE. With verify=False the client accepts any certificate for any host. title: OpenEvolve library API writes the evaluator module into the shared temp dir and adds that dir to sys.path of controller and workers
description: run_evolution() uses a private mkdtemp directory only when output_dir is None and cleanup is True. When the caller passes output_dir or cleanup=False and supplies the evaluator as a callable or a code string, the evaluator pickle, the generated wrapper module and the initial program are written straight into tempfile.gettempdir(). The controller's Evaluator and every worker's Evaluator then insert the evaluator file's directory, which is now the world-writable temp dir, at sys.path[0] (never removed) and import the module from there, with its bytecode cache under <tempdir>/__pycache__. Consequences for another local user of the host: (1) any later import of a not-yet-loaded top-level module in the controller or a worker, including modules resolved while unpickling a cloudpickled evaluator and modules imported by evolved programs that the evaluator loads in-process, is resolved from the temp dir first; (2) if that user owns a pre-created <tempdir>/__pycache__, they can swap the cached .pyc of the evaluator module (source mtime and size are readable) before worker processes import it. Either way their code runs as the operator. The files themselves are created with default umask (world-readable) but cannot be replaced by another user in a sticky temp dir, and their names (uuid4 hex) cannot be pre-created; the evaluated program, which has the operator's uid, can overwrite the pickle, but in this flow it already runs in the worker, so that is not a separate escalation. The repo glue does not use this API (it drives the CLI with a file evaluator), so this affects direct users of the vendored library. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed api.py falls back to tempfile.gettempdir() for the evaluator module (:359-362) and that Evaluator._load_evaluation_function inserts that directory at sys.path[0] (evaluator.py:86-89). The file names carry 8 random hex characters, so the claim rests on the import path, not on predicting a file name. This library API is not used by this repository's glue scripts.

title: OpenEvolve claude.yml starts a secret-bearing agent job for any '@claude' commenter; the only actor gate is inside a floating third-party action tag
description: Scope condition: this workflow is NOT active in the audited repository. SwarmEvolve-cyber has no root .github/ directory, so the file under baselines/openevolve/.github/workflows/ describes the upstream OpenEvolve repository and would only run if copied to a repository root. Evaluated as source for a repository where it is active: the job runs on issue_comment, issues (opened/assigned), pull_request_review and pull_request_review_comment, and its only condition is that the comment, review or issue text contains '@claude'. There is no author_association or actor check, so on a public repository any GitHub account can start the job by commenting on or opening an issue. issue_comment and issues events run in the base-repository context, so the job receives secrets.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN and id-token: write, and hands both to anthropics/claude-code-action at the mutable tag 'beta'. title: OpenEvolve manual-mode endpoints let any client that can reach the visualizer port supply the LLM reply that is then executed
description:
When OpenEvolve runs in manual mode, each LLM call is written as a task file and the run waits for a matching answer file. The visualizer's manual blueprint lists pending task ids, returns each prompt, and accepts an answer by form POST, all without authentication and without any Origin or Host validation. The answer text is returned to the framework as the model reply, converted into a child program and passed to the evaluator, which runs it under the operator's account.

The lower-trust principal is anyone other than the operator who can read responses from the port. Source shows three: (1) another local user on a shared run host, since the default bind is loopback, which every local account can reach; (2) a network client, if the operator starts the visualizer with a non-loopback --host; (3) a web page in the operator's browser that uses DNS rebinding, since any Host header is accepted. Each can list task ids, read the prompts, and post an answer. The first answer written wins, so the operator's own answer for that task is ignored.

A blind cross-site form POST alone does not work: the task id is a random uuid4 and the listing is not readable cross-origin. That narrower claim was refuted from source and is not part of this candidate.

Preconditions: llm.manual_mode must be enabled (it is off by default and is not set by baselines/run_openevolve.py), and the visualizer must be running with --path pointing at the live run directory. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed api_tasks lists task ids and api_task_answer writes the answer with no authentication, Origin or Host check (scripts/manual.py:136-142,159-177), and that manual mode is opt-in (config.py:138 default False; not set by baselines/run_openevolve.py). With manual mode off there is no consumer for the answer.

The only check on the answer route is that the task file exists, and the task id needed to pass it is published by the unauthenticated listing route on the same server. No token, Origin check or Host allowlist binds the answer to the operator.

title: OpenEvolve visualizer writes LLM replies, prompts and artifacts into the page as HTML without escaping
description:
The visualizer sidebar escapes program code but not the Prompts tab. The selected prompt entry, which can be the system prompt, the user prompt, the raw model reply ('responses') or the artifacts JSON, is placed inside a 
 element by string interpolation and assigned to innerHTML. Markup in that text is parsed by the browser, so an inline event handler such as an onerror attribute on an img tag runs script in the visualizer's origin.

The source is the lowest-trust data in the system. The raw model reply is logged verbatim with each program (prompt logging is on by default), the user prompt quotes earlier generated code and program output, and the artifacts entry is the tail of the evaluated program's stdout in this repository's glue. The victim is the operator's browser, which may be on a different machine from the run host (for example through a forwarded port), or anyone who opens a checkpoint directory produced by someone else.

Reaching the main sink needs ordinary inspection steps: select a node, open the Prompts tab and choose the 'user', 'responses' or 'artifacts' entry. title: OpenEvolve static export embeds run data in an inline script without HTML-safe encoding, so '</script>' in generated text injects markup
description:
The --static-output option writes a self-contained index.html. It serialises all programs, prompts, model replies and artifacts with jsonify and concatenates the result into an inline <script> element. JSON serialisation does not escape '<'. The HTML parser ends a script element at the first '</script' regardless of JavaScript string context, so any string value containing that sequence closes the data script, and whatever follows is parsed as HTML.

Program code, model replies and program output are all LLM-derived, so a generated program or reply that contains '</script><script>...' runs script when the exported page is opened. No click is needed. The export is meant to be served or shared (the tool prints a hint to serve it with a web server), so the affected principal is whoever opens the export, in whatever origin hosts it.

The same defect also corrupts the export for benign programs that merely contain the text '</script>'. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed run_static_export builds `<script>window.STATIC_DATA = {data_json};</script>` from jsonify(data).get_data(as_text=True) (scripts/visualizer.py:158-160). Whether that serializer leaves `</script>` intact is behaviour of the installed Flask (pinned 3.1.3, not vendored) and must be observed.
claimed_root_cause: run_static_export builds an inline script by string concatenation of jsonify output. That output is plain JSON, not the HTML-safe form produced by the tojson template filter, so '<', '>' and '&' are not escaped for the script-data context.

title: ShinkaEvolve runner unpickles results_dir/bandit_state.pkl on resume, a file the evaluated program can write
description: When a ShinkaEvolve run is resumed (same results_dir, programs.sqlite with last_iteration > 0) and LLM bandit selection is enabled (framework default 'ucb'), the runner process loads <results_dir>/bandit_state.pkl with pickle.load. Evaluated programs are stored and executed under the same results_dir (<results_dir>/gen_N/main.py) as plain subprocesses, so LLM-generated code can write that file; whatever it pickles is executed inside the runner process at the next resume, after the evaluation job that wrote it has ended or been killed, and on whatever host or account performs the resume. Load failures are swallowed with a warning, so the run continues normally. Scope limits established from source: the load happens once at resume start-up, never periodically; the runner overwrites the file every 5 completed generations and at normal end, so a planted file survives only if it is the last write; the repo glue disables the bandit (llm_dynamic_selection: None) and uses a fresh timestamped directory, so this is reachable with the vendored framework's own defaults or examples, not through baselines/run_baseline.sh. With the local job backend the evaluated program already has the operator's uid and full filesystem access, so the pickle adds a boundary crossing only where the program's writes are otherwise confined to the results tree (the slurm_docker backend with the results directory mounted) or where a results directory is resumed on another host or account. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed pickle.load in load_state (llm/prioritization.py:218-220) and the gate in _load_bandit_state: it returns early when llm_selection is None (core/async_runner.py:627-628). This repository's glue sets llm_dynamic_selection to None (baselines/run_shinkaevolve.py:46), so the default flow here does not reach the sink. A generated program already runs as the operator, so the boundary that matters is a results directory received from someone else and then resumed.

title: shinka-inspect context bundle lets generated program text and program stdout escape their code fences in the file a coding agent is told to load
description: The shinka-inspect skill builds a Markdown 'context bundle' from a ShinkaEvolve results database and instructs the coding agent to load it as its planning context. Two fields in that bundle are authored by the lowest-trust principal in the system: `code` (the LLM-generated program) and `text_feedback` (in this repository's glue, the last 1500 characters the generated program printed). The renderer places each inside a fixed three-backtick fence and does nothing else: no escaping of backtick runs, no fence sized to the content, no marker that the content is untrusted. A program that contains or prints a line of three backticks ends the fence, and everything after it is emitted as ordinary top-level Markdown next to the framework-authored 'Run Metadata' and 'Ranking' sections, so it is indistinguishable from bundle structure or operator notes. The consumer is a different principal with different authority: the operator's coding agent (Claude Code/Codex per the docs), which the sibling shinka-run skill drives through shell commands and, on request, an autonomous multi-batch loop. The script also accepts any results directory or SQLite path, so a database produced in a contained backend, on another machine, or by another person reaches the same agent context. Attacker: whoever controls generated program text or its stdout (a mutation model endpoint, including the documented local/<model>@http(s)://host form, or the author of a shared results DB). Affected principal: the operator, through the agent session's tool authority. This is reported as needs_validation because only the delimiter failure is deterministic and source-visible; whether an agent acts on the escaped text is runtime behaviour, and when generation ran unsandboxed on the same host the generated program already executed as the operator, which limits the added authority to what only the agent session holds. Reviewer note: Not re-traced line by line by the parent. Kept because the locally testable part is deterministic: whether program text containing a backtick run closes the fence in the rendered bundle. What an agent then does with that text is not part of the claim to be reproduced.

title: Every JSON endpoint answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, letting any web page the operator visits read run data through the operator's browser
description: Lower-trust principal: a web page from an unrelated origin opened in the browser the operator uses for the web UI (including when the operator correctly uses an SSH tunnel and a firewalled host). Accepted action: a simple cross-origin GET (fetch or XHR without credentials or custom headers) to http://localhost:<port>/... Control that should stop it: the browser same-origin policy, which the server switches off by sending Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on every JSON response; there is no Origin check and no secret in the URL. Crossed boundary: foreign web origin to operator data. Readable cross-origin: /list_databases, /get_programs, /get_programs_summary, /get_program_details (program source), /get_system_prompts, /get_meta_files, /get_meta_content, /get_plots, /get_database_stats, and, combined with shinka-webui/db-path-traversal, Shinka databases and meta files outside the served directory. Not readable cross-origin: /plot_file/ bodies, the PDF download, error bodies and static files (no CORS header). The page needs the port number; 8000 is the default and 8888 is the documented value. Reviewer note: Parent review confirmed send_json_response sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (visualization.py:1681) for every JSON endpoint; the server uses no credentials, so any origin the operator's browser visits can read these responses if the browser can reach the port.

DEFAULT_PORT is 8000, a predictable target for a foreign page.

title: Meta summary text is converted to HTML without sanitisation and rendered by wkhtmltopdf on the server when a PDF is requested
description: Lower-trust principal: the author of meta_<N>.txt, which in a normal run is the meta-summariser model's output and in a shared-results scenario is whoever produced the results directory the operator is viewing. Accepted input: the file text. Control that should stop it: none; Python-Markdown passes raw HTML through and the result is interpolated into a full HTML document. Sink: that document is written to a temp file and opened by wkhtmltopdf (JavaScript enabled by default, file:// origin) or, failing that, pandoc. Crossed boundary: file content to a headless browser running with the web UI process's filesystem and network position. Any GET /download_meta_pdf triggers it, including from an unauthenticated network client, and the rendered PDF is returned to the requester. If the installed wkhtmltopdf permits local file access or network requests from a local document, injected markup such as an iframe/img/script could place local file content into the PDF or make requests to internal addresses. Bounds established from source: the subprocess calls use argument lists with temp-file paths only, so there is no command injection; the request-supplied 'generation' value is also interpolated unescaped into the document but is reachable only when a file literally named meta_<value>.txt exists; wkhtmltopdf and pandoc are optional external tools that are not installed by the package, and when both are missing the raw text is returned instead. Note that on the host where the evolution itself runs, generated programs already execute as the same user, so the added reach matters mainly when results are viewed on a different machine or come from a third party.
claimed_root_cause: _generate_pdf builds the renderer input by concatenating markdown.markdown(meta_text) (raw HTML allowed) and the request's generation string into an HTML template with no escaping or sanitising, then hands it to a browser-engine converter without disabling JavaScript, local file access or network access.

An unauthenticated GET /download_meta_pdf reads the meta file text and passes it to _generate_pdf (line 913).
markdown.markdown converts the text; raw HTML in the input is preserved.
The converted HTML is interpolated unescaped into the document body, which is written to a temp .html file at line 1501.
wkhtmltopdf renders the temp file with only page-size and margin options; the output PDF is returned to the requester.

evidence.description: Only the 'extra' and 'nl2br' extensions are enabled; no sanitising extension or post-filter is applied.
The wkhtmltopdf argument list has no --disable-javascript, --disable-local-file-access or --disable-external-links option.

The request's generation/processed_count string is also placed unescaped in the document title and heading (line 1490), bounded by the file-existence check at line 902.
The converter output is sent back to whoever made the request.

reason: No principal gains a result across a boundary. The author of the meta text is the model, which never receives the PDF: it is returned to the requester. The model's generated programs already run as the operator by design, so script or file inclusion inside wkhtmltopdf adds no capability for it. A requester who can reach the endpoint already has the broader file reads recorded as shinka-webui/plot-file-unrestricted-read and shinka-webui/db-path-traversal. The command line is a fixed argv list, so there is no command injection. Kept as a hardening note: escape or sanitise the HTML and pass --disable-local-file-access / --disable-javascript.

title: /plot_file/ returns any file under the search root (by default the launch directory that holds .env) and its prefix check admits sibling directories and symlinks
description: Lower-trust principal: any client that can send an HTTP GET to the web UI port (the server listens on all interfaces without authentication; see shinka-webui/wildcard-bind-no-auth). Accepted input: the URL path after /plot_file/. Control that should stop it: the 'Security check: ensure the path is within search_root' in handle_serve_plot_file. Crossed boundary: network client to operator files. The handler is meant to serve plot images that /get_plots lists (png/gif/jpg/jpeg only), but it applies no extension or sub-directory restriction, so every regular file under search_root is returned as application/octet-stream. search_root defaults to the current working directory, and the documented quick start runs 'shinka_visualize --port 8888' with no directory from the project/launch directory, which is also where the docs tell the operator to keep a .env file with provider API keys and where shinka loads it from. GET /plot_file/.env would then return those keys. Three further weaknesses in the same check: (1) containment is a string startswith on abspath values with no trailing separator, so a root of .../results also admits .../results_old/ or .../results.bak via '../results_old/...'; (2) abspath does not resolve symlinks, so a link placed inside the root is followed out of it; (3) existence is tested before containment, so 404 versus 403 tells the client whether an arbitrary host path exists. Limits: paths outside the root that do not share its string prefix are refused; the response carries no CORS header, so a cross-origin page cannot read it directly (a same-origin script, see shinka-webui/dom-xss-llm-derived-fields, can). Reviewer note: Parent review re-read handle_serve_plot_file (visualization.py:981-1020): the only containment is abspath(...).startswith(abspath(search_root)) at :997, with no trailing separator and no file-type allowlist; search_root defaults to the current working directory (main(), :1750-1757).
claimed_root_cause: handle_serve_plot_file treats 'inside search_root by string prefix' as the whole authorisation decision: it has no file-type or plots-directory allowlist, compares un-normalised prefixes without a path separator, uses abspath instead of realpath, and checks existence before containment.

title: Web UI listens on all interfaces with no authentication while the documentation describes access through an SSH tunnel to localhost
description: Lower-trust principal: any host that can open a TCP connection to the operator's machine on the chosen port (other users of a shared GPU server or cluster network, other devices on the same LAN). Accepted action: any GET request. Control that should stop it: none in source; the listening address is the empty string (all IPv4 interfaces) and there is no option to change it, no token, and no Host or Origin validation. The documentation's remote workflow starts the server on the remote machine and reaches it through 'ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888', which only requires a loopback listener and leads an operator to assume the service is tunnel-only; the same page separately shows a cluster tunnel to a compute node's own address and a one-line 'never expose ports publicly' note. Crossed boundary: network client to operator data. Affected resources: every evolved program, metric, stored LLM prompt/response and log in the served databases, system prompts, meta summaries, and through the two file-handling candidates (shinka-webui/plot-file-unrestricted-read, shinka-webui/db-path-traversal) any file under the launch directory such as .env and Shinka databases elsewhere on the host. The absence of Host validation also leaves the loopback case open to DNS rebinding from a web page. This candidate is limited to exposure of the read-only API; no state-changing endpoint exists.
